paras: The shooting of John Taylor at Castle Haynes was the killing of a Black convict by guards who fired on twelve prisoners escaping from the New Hanover County chain-gang stockade, six miles from Wilmington, North Carolina, early on April 20, 1903. Two other escapees, a white convict, J. P. Hughes, and a Black convict, Forney George, were reported wounded. The break came shortly after a grand jury described the camp as infested with vermin, and an opposition paper in Clinton used it to attack the county's Democratic administration.

New Hanover County held its chain-gang convicts in a stockade at Castle Haynes, from which guards took them out in the morning to work. Shortly before the break, a county grand jury reported the camp's clothing so full of vermin that jurors had to stop their carriage to pick the insects off their coats.

Early on Monday, April 20, as guards were bringing a gang of about fifty convicts out of the stockade, twelve of them, three white and nine Black, broke and ran for the woods. According to the Times-Dispatch correspondent, one guard ordered the remaining prisoners onto their knees and held them while the other guards opened fire on the fugitives. Taylor, who was serving twelve months for larceny, described by the Times-Dispatch as stealing chickens, was shot dead almost instantly. Accounts of George's wound differed: the Times-Dispatch said he and Hughes were "shot in the back, but escaped," while the News and Observer reported him wounded only "according to reports by convicts captured."

The break was said to have been planned by Harrison Martin, a white convict sentenced the week before for an assault on a widow. The county commissioners offered rewards of $50 each for Martin and Hughes and $20 for each Black escapee, and a sheriff's posse searched the countryside. Several men were retaken that day, two of them by "colored guards" posted at the Northeast River bridge. Before daylight on April 21, Martin and two Black convicts, wet, cold and hungry after hours in a swamp, surrendered at the stockade.

Hughes's fate remained uncertain after the break; the News and Observer believed him badly wounded, and the Times-Dispatch reported it was "believed that he died in the woods of his wound." He was alive in late June, when two men from Whiteville captured him at Lebanon in Columbus County and collected the county's $50 reward. By then every escapee had been returned except a Black convict serving a short term from Craven County. No report of an inquest into Taylor's death or of any inquiry into the guards' shooting appears in the coverage.

The white press learned of the shooting from two Wilmington specials, one to the Richmond Times-Dispatch under the headline "Wild Dash for Liberty" and one to the Raleigh News and Observer as "A Dash for Freedom by Twelve in Stripes." Both narrated the guards' fire without comment, and the Times-Dispatch text went out on the wire, appearing as "A Fatal Dash for Liberty" in the Indianapolis Journal and in briefer form in Louisiana and South Carolina papers.

In North Carolina, The Caucasian of Clinton reprinted the News and Observer dispatch with the subhead "Some of the Convicts at Castle Haynes Leaves the Filthy Vermin Behind Them." A week later its editorial "From Lice to Liberty—Some to Death" blamed the "democratic reform administration" and called the break "fatal to one or two of his fellows." The editorial complained that some escapees had been retaken "in the white city of Wilmington by negro officers," but it did not question the guards' shooting.
The only Black-press report, in the Savannah Tribune on April 25, carried the wire account under the headline "Convicts Take Leg Bail," naming no one and adding no comment.

The two Wilmington correspondents disagreed on Martin's sentence (four years in the Times-Dispatch, two in the News and Observer) and on whether George came from "Newbern" or Columbus County. The News and Observer had Charles Bryan captured on April 20 but at large the next day. While the Caucasian editorial wrote of "some dead," the June report spoke of "the killing of one," and no paper named a second death.

bases: Prison guards at the county chain-gang stockade shot and killed a Black convict and wounded two others as twelve convicts ran from custody (A2, A5).

accounts.label: News and Observer Wilmington correspondent
accounts.gist: Taylor was shot and almost instantly killed by the guards; Hughes was wounded as he ran; George was wounded according to captured convicts. In June Hughes was captured alive.

accounts.gist: Their reports were the source for Forney George's wound.

accounts.label: Clinton Caucasian editorial
accounts.gist: The convicts fled lice, filth and 'miscegenation' imposed by the Democratic administration; the break was 'fatal to one or two'.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: Twelve convicts broke from the Castle Haynes stockade; one Black man killed, a white man and a Black man wounded; no names.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'Wild Dash for Liberty' and 'One Killed Instantly', describing the guards' fire without comment.
The News and Observer headlined 'A Dash for Freedom by Twelve in Stripes' and focused on recaptures and rewards.
Wire versions ran as 'A Fatal Dash for Liberty' and 'Escape Of Convicts' in Indiana, Louisiana and South Carolina papers.
The Clinton Caucasian blamed the Democratic administration's 'vermin' camp for the break, lamenting deaths, but resented the recapture 'by negro officers' and did not fault the guards' shooting.
The Savannah Tribune ran the unnamed wire brief as 'Convicts Take Leg Bail' with no comment.
